title: Communicating a breaking change on a public API
situation: Your v3 API drops two v2 fields, which is a breaking change. Of the three downstream teams, one has refused to upgrade for a long time. The contract SLA requires 90 days' notice.

options.text: Follow the 90-day process and publish a deprecation notice
Privately agree a longer compatibility layer with the reluctant team
Switch v2 off and force them to upgrade

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
situation: They are grateful, take the post down, and become more careful about information security. Three months later someone else makes a worse mistake of the same kind: a log snippet containing sensitive customer data, picked up by an external crawler. Security's investigation finds that you knew about the first incident and did not report it, and they question your security awareness.

options.text: Admit you handled it badly, accept the company's sanction, and propose a 'good-faith warning' route for first minor incidents
Argue that the two incidents differed in severity, and that your call was reasonable in context

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
situation: A week later they still have not delivered, and your stopgap cannot fully cover the gap. In the project update your risk warning looks late. A VP asks why you are only saying so now.

options.text: Own your misjudgement of the risk, and ask for a more formal way of tracking cross-team dependencies
Point to the other team's history of slipping, and stress you could only judge what you could see

title: The company tries to keep you after you look elsewhere
situation: You take the rise and keep looking. It shows. Your manager finds out you are still interviewing, trust collapses, and the project and the promotion hint are withdrawn. You keep the money you were already given. You are still here, in a worse position.

options.text: Stop sitting on the fence, commit, and win trust back by being consistent
Keep both options vaguely alive, one more day at a time

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: A new manager is hired in over your team, with a strong background and a style nothing like the last one. They do not know you yet. Some people are already sucking up to them; others are watching coldly. You start from nothing, and they will control your reviews and your prospects. What is your first move?

options.text: Lead with the work: explain clearly what you are doing and ask what they expect, without grovelling or bristling
Rush to pick their side and lay the flattery on
Watch them coldly, resist, and talk about how much better the last one was

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
situation: In a routine review you find a potential security hole: under certain conditions, an attacker could reach another user's data. Fixing it means rebuilding the core authorisation module. That touches much of the system, needs a long round of testing, and will probably delay a release that is about to go out. Security rates it medium: fix it soon, but don't block the release. Product is firmly against moving the date, since nobody has complained about it.

options.text: Block the release until the hole is fully fixed and has passed a security audit
Accept a later fix, but put temporary mitigations and monitoring in first

title: Christmas-party rehearsals eating your evenings
situation: You stay late every night so you are not the weak link. Your actual work stacks up, and two month-end deliveries go wrong enough that your manager names you. A polished dance number does not make up for it. You can see you got the balance wrong.

options.text: Reorder your priorities: catch up on the work and put a limit on rehearsals
Keep putting rehearsals first and let the work wait

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: You get up and run a quick game for the whole room. It goes down better than you expected. People are laughing, and your manager gives you a thumbs-up. Afterwards the host tries to keep you up there for the next part.

options.text: Quit while you are ahead: hand the stage back and return to your table
Ride the moment and keep hosting, even as you start to run out of steam

title: The pay-review pot is tight and you are competing for a rise
situation: You make your case with a solid summary of what you have delivered and a plan for what you will contribute next. Your manager accepts that you are capable, but says the others are strong too and there is a balance to strike. Then you hear a rival has been talking you down behind your back.

options.text: Do not hit back: keep letting your results speak, and set the record straight if needed without attacking them
Get angry, and start talking them down in return

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You survive a round of redundancies. Several colleagues are gone, and your manager asks you to cover the urgent part of their work for a short while and to come back with what should wait. Your pay has not changed. Until that conversation happens, you are carrying more. How do you handle it?

options.text: Prioritise the new work, discuss resources and limits with your manager, and push for support or something in return
Take the lot in silence and carry it at any cost
Push back by coasting: the more that arrives, the more you half-do it

title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
situation: You joined the mockery aimed at Chris himself, and the thread, with the screenshot and the jokes, was forwarded into channels that have nothing to do with the complaint. IT traces the chain. Handing the screenshot to HR, a representative, a union or a solicitor for the complaint is not part of what is being looked at.

options.text: Own up that you joined in
Deny it

title: Whether to warn that the sprint is overcommitted
situation: In sprint planning, Product brings in far more story points than the team can handle. Your manager looks at you: “Can we do it?” Everyone else stays quiet.

options.text: Use the numbers to show the team is over capacity, and suggest cutting scope
Nod and take it on
Raise it privately with your manager after the meeting

title: The pay rise did not come through — coast in protest?
situation: Your request for a pay rise got nowhere this time. Your manager only said 'let's see'. You feel deflated, and your energy for the work drops. What next?

options.text: Hold your nerve, keep delivering, build your case for next time, and agree a date to revisit it
Protest by coasting and drag your feet on everything you can
In a huff, tell the whole office 'I'll walk', with no actual plan

title: Annual bonus cut and paid in instalments
situation: The company announces that the annual bonus, which your contract describes as discretionary, is being reduced and paid over several quarters, citing 'cash-flow management'. A contractual sum could not be cut like this without your agreement. As it is, your expected pay takes a hit, and the move says something about how the business is doing.

options.text: Take it as a warning: look hard at the company's prospects and adjust your own plans
Complain in public and lead the moaning
Tell yourself at least they are still paying it, and try not to think about it

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: Afterwards you book fifteen minutes with your manager and show how the work maps to business metrics. They soften: “Next time, put the business value on page one.” You still sense the rest of the team thinks engineering work does not count. You need to decide whether to fight for the team's visibility.

options.text: Push to get your work into team OKRs or the quarterly highlights
Keep to your own patch and stop speaking for the team

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: InfoSec opens an investigation. Your call records with Felix are pulled.

options.text: Cooperate with the investigation
Deny it

title: Burnout, and the urge to coast
situation: You are exhausted, and one thought keeps coming back: pack it in and just coast. It is a classic sign of burnout, and decisions made on impulse now are the ones people regret. How do you deal with it?

options.text: Take it seriously: a few days' annual leave, a saner pace, and a workload talk with your manager if needed
Bottle it, pretend you are fine, and keep running on empty
Give in to the urge to coast and start phoning the work in

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You rework the lot without pinning down what went wrong. Their spoken requests stay vague, and version two is sent back as well. The team is exhausted, so are you, and the real problem is still there: nothing is clearly signed off.

options.text: Stop the blind rework and put a proper sign-off in place before going further
Keep reworking on demand, exactly as they say

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
situation: Sonya is satisfied. A week later a recruiter contacts Leo. Your manager starts asking where it came from.

options.text: Admit you gave her a vague outline over dinner
Deny it

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: Faye at the next desk has a heavy cold. She is coughing constantly and has almost lost her voice, but she is still in: 'The milestone's tight, I can't drop the ball.' The whole open-plan floor can hear every cough, and two people have started sneezing. She sees it as doing her duty, but there is a real risk she will pass it on. You are on the same project.

options.text: Check in privately, ask her to go home, and offer to cover the urgent part
Tell your manager her coming in ill is a health risk, and suggest sick leave while the team covers
Put on a mask, move away from the noise and the germs, and say nothing

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: The release slips a day. Your manager asks why.

options.text: Hold a review and add a release checklist
Just say the merge went wrong

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You set out what each of them needs and suggest a fixed middle temperature, a small screen to keep the draught off Maya, and a desk fan for Hugh. Both feel looked after, and most of the heat goes out of the row. To make it happen, someone has to ask facilities for the extras.

options.text: Take the lead with facilities and get the extras in
You had the idea. They can chase it themselves

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You are at a client dinner. After a few drinks, one of their senior people starts making jokes that cross a line — pointed, sexual remarks aimed at Chloe, a woman on your side of the table. Her laugh is tight and she looks trapped. They are an important account. Everyone else is pretending it is banter. The table is waiting to see what you do.

options.text: Change the subject without a scene, pull the talk back to the work, and give Chloe a way out
Join in and laugh along, to keep the ‘atmosphere’
Say firmly that the remark is not on, and bring the talk back to the work

title: You notice a remote colleague is often offline
situation: Your manager reviews the remote-working data, spots the unusual away time, and asks whether you knew.

options.text: Say you had noticed they were stretched, and suggest the manager speak to them directly
Say you did not know, and offer nothing further

title: Invited to shadow a senior planning meeting
situation: Your friend over-reads the hint, spreads anxiety through their team, and even starts looking for other jobs. The CTO hears that details of the meeting have leaked and starts tracing the source.

options.text: Go to the CTO, admit you shared no detail but may have hinted too strongly, and take responsibility
Deny passing anything on, and suggest their anxiety may have come from somewhere else

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: The claim goes through. Next month a spot audit flags your late-dinner line as 'possible non-compliance'. Finance asks you to explain or repay.

options.text: Repay it, admit you should have been stricter, and promise to stick to the policy
Say you followed team custom, and suggest Finance stop chasing individuals and set a clear rule

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: Intern Quinn accidentally sends "Chris changes his mind like a rollercoaster" to the whole 200-person department. Two minutes later Quinn is in tears at your desk: "What do I do? I can't recall it." Chris is on the thread and has already read it.

options.text: Go with Quinn to apologise to Chris in person straight away
Suggest sending a follow-up claiming the account was hacked
Stay out of it and leave Quinn to deal with it
Call IT first and ask whether the email can still be recalled

title: A chatty, skiving colleague eating into your time
situation: Luke, a teammate, has taken to hovering at your desk for half-hour chats: gossip, moaning, memes. You can tell their own workload is light and they mostly want someone to skive with. You have a critical module due for QA today and have already been interrupted three times. You need to decide how to handle it.

options.text: Tell them directly but politely that you need to focus today and to come back later
Put headphones on, look busy, and give them the cold shoulder
Chat for a few minutes, then steer back to work and mention today's deadline
Tell your manager that Luke keeps breaking your concentration

title: Whether to invest in a CI automation suite
situation: CI goes live and the team's merge speed improves markedly. New joiners find the configuration harder than expected, though, and the last two PRs sat blocked for hours. A senior colleague suggests loosening the gates so people can get used to the workflow, then tightening them later. You need to decide how strict CI should be.

options.text: Keep the strict gates and make the team meet the higher bar
Loosen the thresholds so the team can ease into the CI workflow

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: Your candour sparks a team discussion about labelling AI-written code. Your manager asks you to lead on drafting a guideline.

options.text: Take it on and push for a team standard on being open about AI use
Suggest a more experienced colleague lead it, and stay involved

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
situation: They say they do remember the chat, thought it was just thinking out loud, and had not realised how close it was to what they had in mind. They promise to credit you in later docs. The VP's impression of who proposed it will be hard to undo.

options.text: Accept the promise. Credit in the docs is enough
Ask them to say at the next update that the idea originally came from you

title: At the demo, your manager praises Product and not engineering
situation: At the sprint demo, your manager says the product design was excellent and does not mention the late nights engineering put in. The client is on the call.

options.text: After the demo, email the client (cc'd) with the technical highlights
Jump in on the call to explain how engineering built it
Say nothing

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: Ethan’s bonus is roughly halved. He blocks you for three months. Some people on the team call you tough.

options.text: Try to explain the constraints of the rating system
Accept that the friendship is over

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: The team has one place at an industry conference. It is a good trip with plenty of visibility, and word is it will go to you or Jo. Your manager catches you in the kitchen and asks, as if in passing, 'How has Jo been lately? Do you think she's the right person to represent the team?' You can tell they are testing how you compete. The list is due next week.

options.text: Give Jo fair credit for her strengths and say she would be a good fit
Praise Jo, and briefly add your own recent relevant work
Say you each have strengths, and suggest choosing whoever fits the brief best
Hint at gaps in Jo's recent work

title: A colleague accidentally posts internal architecture online
situation: Browsing GitHub, you find that a colleague has posted an architecture diagram of an internal system in a public technical thread. Names have been removed, but anyone who knows the company would recognise it. It is clearly an accident: they were in a hurry to get help with a hard problem. Report it, and they may face disciplinary action. Warn them privately, and you may later be treated as having known and said nothing.

options.text: Help them take the post down, then report the accidental disclosure to security and say it was a mistake
Message them privately to take it down now, on the understanding that it goes no further

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: Your manager praises you for raising it face to face, then gets defensive about the substance. They explain why those decisions were reasonable, and hint that 'you're only seeing a slice'.

options.text: Stand by what you observed, admit your view is partial, and suggest more openness about how decisions are made
Ease off, admit you may have lacked some information, and say you still rate their management overall

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: Dual-write means building a sync-and-check tool this week, which pushes out a request from the rewards centre.

options.text: Take it on and ask your manager to drop the other work
Refuse to build the tool, and force a straight choice between delaying and rushing

title: Should you leave the company a bad Glassdoor review?
situation: You have a stack of grievances and fancy leaving a low score and a rant on Glassdoor, as a warning for the next person and a chance to get it off your chest.

options.text: If you write, stick to facts: no exaggeration, no confidential detail, no personal attacks
Write a long, emotional recap of every grievance, including unverified claims
Hold off, and use the frustration to decide properly whether to stay or go

title: A job spec from the big tech firm you have always wanted to join
situation: You come across a role that closely matches yours at a company you have always wanted to work for. Reading the spec, you feel envious and a bit anxious, because you are not there yet. What do you do with that feeling?

options.text: Use the spec as a yardstick and close the gaps in your current role until you could get it
Spend the days daydreaming about leaving, refreshing job boards, and letting the day job drift
Envy it and do nothing, telling yourself you would never get there anyway

title: Your manager blames 'the climate' to keep your increase down
situation: In the pay-review conversation you name a figure and your manager waves it off: 'The climate is grim this year. The whole company is tightening its belt — that increase isn't realistic.' The wider economy is being used as cover to talk you down.

options.text: Acknowledge the climate, then bring the conversation back to your actual contribution and market rates
Lose heart at 'the climate' and cut your ask to something tiny
Get heated and snap that the climate is nothing to do with you, and the conversation turns into a row

title: You bring an outside offer back to negotiate pay
situation: You have a real offer from another company, paying more. You are not set on leaving, and would prefer to use it as leverage for the rise you think you are owed here. Bringing an offer into a pay conversation can help or hurt you, depending on how you use it.

options.text: Be straight: you want to stay, here is what the market pays, and would they review your pay
Use the offer as an ultimatum: “Match this number or I go today”
Inflate the offer and quote your manager a much higher number

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: Finance clears your claim quickly. Colleagues notice the total is well below what people usually claim and rib you over lunch: 'A bit too honest, aren't you? You've left money on the table.'

options.text: Say it is your own choice, and remind people what the policy actually allows
Smile it off. Keep your own standard without commenting on anyone else's

title: The client praises a feature you did not build
situation: In the Cedar Retail project review, the client’s procurement director says: “This real-time stock sync can forecast next week’s bestsellers. That’s ahead of the market.” What you actually shipped is next-day (T+1) batch sync, and forecasting is on next year’s roadmap. Kim, the product manager, catches your eye. Your manager smiles and nods. The review is going smoothly, and about £80,000 of the contract is still waiting to be paid.

options.text: Say in the room that what is live is next-day sync, and forecasting is a later proposal
Keep quiet in the room and clarify in writing after the meeting
Stay silent and let the review pass

title: Funding and listing rumours — bet on the share options?
situation: Word is the company is raising money or heading for a listing. People talk as if the share options will make them rich, and they tell you to 'hang on a few more years for the options — don't leave'. The rumours are hard to pin down and a payout looks a long way off. You are not sure you should hang a career decision on it.

options.text: Count the share options as a possible bonus and decide on the fundamentals of the job
Turn down a better offer in front of you and stay put for options that have been over-promised
Ignore the options entirely, count only cash, and leave as soon as something better comes up

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
situation: Sienna holds off signing. Two weeks later the change is announced and she thanks you. Your manager senses a leak and starts checking who knew.

options.text: Go to your manager and admit you dropped a vague hint
Stay silent

title: A colleague who comes in ill
situation: Faye is touched but still hesitates: 'I feel bad, you've got your own work.' You take the most urgent part and she goes home. Now your own schedule is packed, the milestone is close, and you are feeling the strain.

options.text: Tell your manager you are covering Faye for now, and ask for a realistic plan
Carry all of it without telling anyone, and work late to catch up

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: At your third lunch you overhear people discussing who will get places on next quarter’s flagship project. Someone floats your name. Someone else says “we never see them.” You need to decide how often to keep going.

options.text: Keep lunching with the team every day
Drop back to Tuesdays and Thursdays once you have the key information

title: Your manager gives you a rise — with a lot more work attached
situation: Your manager offers you a rise, then adds, 'Now that the pay is up, you can take on these extra bits of the business as well.' The increase is real, and so is the extra load. The two may not balance.

options.text: Weigh the extra work against the increase, take what is fair, and say so if it would overload you
Get carried away by the rise and accept every new piece of work without counting the load
Take the rise but quietly dodge the extra work

title: A senior puts their name on an intern’s work
situation: Rowan turns on you in the room. Your manager tells you to “sort it afterwards.” Quinn’s name is added. Rowan freezes you out.

options.text: Walk your manager through the facts and ask for a fair rating
Take on some of Rowan’s work to thaw the relationship

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
situation: Aurora wins. You are named at the awards. Three months later internal audit picks the pack for a spot check and asks you to describe exactly what you contributed to the platform.

options.text: Admit you were not part of the core work
Invent a contribution that matches your manager’s story

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
situation: Harvey is named acting lead and puts you on weekend on-call.

options.text: Take the on-call and keep the relationship
Refuse and draw a line

title: In-house senior architect certification over the weekend
situation: The tech committee is running an in-house senior architect certification this Saturday and Sunday, on your own time. It is optional, and the company covers the fee. Meanwhile, an internal tooling project of yours is due next Tuesday as planned. If you put in extra hours this weekend, you could ship it on Monday morning, which your client contact says would save them a day of integration. You had already planned a weekend away with family. You cannot do all three. How do you spend the weekend?

options.text: Sign up for the certification and spend both days learning properly
Work through the weekend to deliver the project on Monday morning
Stick to the family weekend and pick work up next week as planned

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: You used an AI assistant to generate the core of a complex algorithm, edited it, and opened a pull request. The team has no rule on whether AI contributions need to be flagged. In review a colleague admires how clever the code is — and you realise they have no idea a model wrote the first draft.

options.text: Note in the PR that it was AI-assisted, and explain what you changed
Say nothing extra, and let it read as ordinary engineering

title: School run clashing with overtime
situation: Your child has just started school. Pick-ups and being there for your child both take time, and this project is busy. At this company, staying late has become the norm, and family time and work are clashing.

options.text: Share the load at home, agree some flexibility with the team, and make a formal flexible-working request for the school run
Throw yourself into the project and put family time on hold
Try to do everything perfectly at home and at work, and run yourself into the ground

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: The gamble failed, and you only told them on delivery day that it would be late. The client is furious: 'Why didn't you say? I can't explain this upstairs.' They want an explanation from the company. Your manager is pulled in.

options.text: Apologise in person at once, present a detailed recovery plan, and fix how you communicate
Explain why you were a victim of this too

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: The company health-check results are in, and several of yours are flagged: abnormal liver function, a thyroid nodule recommended for further biopsy, and an ECG noting occasional extra beats. The doctor has written, 'See a specialist promptly; avoid late nights and high stress.' These two weeks are the quarterly delivery sprint, and your module is on the critical path. Going for follow-up tests means handing your work to someone else. What do you do?

options.text: Take leave now for specialist tests and hand over your work cleanly
Push through this delivery and book the follow-up for the end of the month
Decide health checks always scare people, and ignore it

title: You survive a round of cuts and inherit the work
situation: You go through the extra work with your manager: what you can carry, what needs more people or time, and why covering at this level should come with something in return. They like how organised you are and that you have taken it on, give you some support, and note your contribution. Covering becomes a way to prove your value.

options.text: Cover the critical work well, and turn “stepping up” into a case for promotion and a rise
Ease off after the conversation, and do not deliver what you promised

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: A flat no in front of everyone made the client look small. The atmosphere soured, and they think you are 'inflexible and not commercial'. Afterwards they complain to your manager. The request could have been handled more gently.

options.text: Go to the client, smooth things over, explain where the line is, and offer a workable change proposal
Stand firm: 'I wasn't wrong. The contract is the contract'

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You made the call and the row stopped. Maya, who lost out, feels hard done by, thinks you sided with the majority, and is cooler with you afterwards. Shutting the argument down did nothing for the person in the minority.

options.text: Talk to Maya privately and find her a way to keep warm, to soften the blunt call
Majority rules. Nobody needs extra looking after

title: A colleague keeps helping themselves to your snacks
situation: You keep a few snacks in your drawer. Colleague Mia "just grabs a handful" every day, never brings her own, and has never returned the favour. Today she grins, "Yours are the best." It isn't much, but it is starting to grate.

options.text: Joke: "Bring some next time and we can swap", and leave it there
Keep sharing, because you don't like to say anything
Lock the snacks away and stop sharing, without explaining

title: A colleague's clutter takes over the aisle
situation: Leon, who sits next to you, hoards things. Boxes, parcels and gym kit are all over the floor and have slowly taken over the shared aisle between you. You have to turn sideways to get past, and it is a trip hazard. He doesn't seem to see a problem.

options.text: Tell him the aisle is too tight and suggest sorting the clutter together
Squeeze past every day and say nothing
While he is away, pile all of it onto his desk

title: Write down what only you know, or keep it in your head?
situation: You are the only person who really knows a core product area. For two years you have solved the hard problems, and you have never properly written down what you know. Your manager asks you to run a 'knowledge transfer' session and write a proper design document. You can see that if you hand everything over, you become much easier to replace. If you hold it back, the team carries a risk, and your own career has a lower ceiling.

options.text: Document it fully: the design thinking, the traps, and a troubleshooting handbook
Write up the basic architecture, but keep the real troubleshooting and deeper principles to pass on in conversation

title: Grey-area items on a travel expense claim
situation: You have just finished a week on a client site and are putting the expenses together. A few items sit in a grey area: 1) coffees you bought the client as a gift (no VAT receipt, only a till slip); 2) a late dinner you ordered for yourself after overtime (policy covers a 'working meal'; late dinners are not spelled out); 3) the taxi to the airport diverted to pick up a colleague travelling with you (about £3 extra).

options.text: Claim only the flights and hotels, which are clearly within policy, and drop every grey item
Claim as usual, taking colleagues' advice that 'everyone does this, it's fine'

title: A side project blurs the line with company business
situation: Compliance confirms you are not currently in breach, but suggests you sign an extra restrictive-covenant clause limiting how far you can take enterprise services later.

options.text: Accept the terms, so the side project stays within a legal framework
Challenge the extra clause as too broad, and propose a tighter definition of the boundary

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: You refuse bluntly. The host has to paper over an awkward few seconds. The people who were winding you up look silly, and your manager marks you down as “not really a team person.” There was a more graceful way to say no.

options.text: Recover by joining a later group game to show you are still part of things
Sit the rest of the night out with a face like thunder, speaking to nobody

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: An upstream dependency has failed on a project you own. You now know you will be a week late, and the original delivery date is three days away. The client cares a lot about this one and has even put their own name behind it internally. You need to decide how to tell them.

options.text: Tell them at once, with a cause analysis, a recovery plan and a new timetable
Wait until delivery day in case you still make it
Report 'on time', then quietly work late and try to catch up

title: A Glassdoor post about the company is doing the rounds
situation: A tell-all post about the company is spreading fast on Glassdoor, and only half of it is true. People in the team channel are forwarding it and stirring things up, and they ask what you think.

options.text: Don't spread it or take sides, and pay attention only to facts that affect you
Forward it eagerly to every chat, adding your own embellishments
Leave an anonymous comment adding more detail

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
situation: The annual engagement survey says answers are confidential. The portal asks for your staff ID and an SMS code, which may only be there to stop someone submitting twice. The page does not say whether anyone can later trace an answer back to you. You have a long list on Chris, your manager: goalposts that move, taking credit, weekend pings. A colleague believes that last year someone who wrote something sharp was frozen out afterwards.

options.text: Fill it in honestly, with examples and no swearing
Score everything as blandly positive
Set out the moving goalposts, the credit-taking and the weekend messages as plain facts, without insults

title: An intern accidentally emails a rant about the manager
situation: IT shows the account was not hacked. You and Quinn are both investigated.

options.text: Admit you suggested the cover story
Blame Quinn

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: Your manager wants to talk about a 'promotion': a bigger title and a heavier workload, with the pay 'held for now — we'll look at it next year'. It is a better title with no rise: more prestige, more work, same money. The question is whether you take it, and on what terms.

options.text: Weigh what the title is actually worth, and whether it paves the way for a rise, before you negotiate
Get swept up by the title and take the lot without a second thought
Take the missing rise as an insult, refuse on the spot, and leave a sharp remark hanging

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
situation: Production has a critical fault and needs an immediate hotfix. The standard path of code review, staging checks and a confirmed rollback would take about two hours. A client is in the middle of a live promotional stream, and every minute of downtime is a serious loss. The operations lead hints you could ship now and backfill the process later.

options.text: Stick to the full process, and turn on a degraded mode to limit the impact on the client
Ship on a shortened path while the team prepares a rollback and completes the review within an hour

title: An engagement survey that asks for your staff ID
situation: HR pass on “please set dates more clearly” to Chris. He tries two weeks of stand-ups to fix it.

options.text: Acknowledge the improvement in the meeting so that it sticks
Wait and see

title: Choosing a stack for a new module
situation: You need to pick a stack for a new module. You could write the team's mature stack in your sleep, and it would almost certainly deliver on time. There is also a more modern framework with an active community that fits better in the long term. But neither you nor the team has used it in production, so expect pitfalls and an uncertain first release. The module is not on the critical path and the timetable is fairly generous. Your manager leaves the decision entirely to you. A proposal is due at next week's architecture huddle.

options.text: Adopt the new framework and use this low-risk module to build experience
Stick with the mature stack and put reliable delivery first

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: In the quarterly anonymous team survey you left specific suggestions about your manager's style, including some criticism. Afterwards they tell the team that 'anonymous feedback is cowardly — if there's a problem you should say it to my face'. A few days later they take you aside: 'I don't know who it was, but I think you're the most likely to have written those detailed points. I'd like to hear what you actually think.'

options.text: Own it, walk through the feedback in person, and offer constructive suggestions
Deny it, suggest other possible sources, and protect the anonymity

title: After dinner, karaoke with someone on the promotion panel
situation: You sing two songs. Helen says you are down to earth. At 1am she asks privately whether you are interested in Polaris — you cannot tell if it is drink talking.

options.text: Show interest and ask how to prepare for promotion
Talk about the project and leave promotion out, so it does not look transactional

title: Dependency upgrade breaks the build
situation: Dependabot auto-upgrades a transitive dependency and main goes red. You suspect a breaking patch.

options.text: Revert immediately, pin the version, and find the cause
Hack the code to match the new version
Disable Dependabot

title: Should you take a transitional role mixing engineering and management?
situation: Your manager suggests a transitional role: managing two or three people while keeping part of your engineering work. It would let you test the move from individual contributor towards management with less at stake. It could also mean doing neither job well. Do you take it?

options.text: Take it as a low-risk trial of management, and plan how you will split your time
Play it safe, refuse any people responsibility, and stay a pure individual contributor
Take it but never split your time, try to do all of both jobs, and fail at both

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
situation: The internal tech forum is calling for posts. You have a method for payments circuit breaking and graceful degradation that you have never shared, and it is what makes you hard to replace on the team. Publishing it would probably get a reaction from the CTO and help your promotion case, but colleagues could copy it quickly.

options.text: Publish the full version and build a personal brand
Post a cut-down version and keep the core parameters back
Don't share it, and keep it to yourself

title: A junior asks to pair on your state machine
situation: Intern Alex asks for two hours this afternoon to pair, so he can understand a state machine you wrote. You have a bug that needs to be fixed by four.

options.text: Reschedule: pair first, then fix the bug
Point him at the docs and comments and let him work through it
Pair for an hour and do the rest asynchronously

title: How thorough to be in code review as the team grows
situation: Since the team expanded, the weekly review queue has jumped from five or six PRs to more than thirty. As technical owner, you are the named reviewer on most of the critical modules. Each PR now takes 30–40 minutes; one or two hours a day disappear into review. A new colleague's PR is in your queue: the logic is sound, but there are plenty of nits: style, edge cases, naming. You need to decide how detailed this review should be.

options.text: Review line by line and list every improvement
Focus on core logic and risk, and leave the nits to the author

title: Abnormal health-check results: push through or see a doctor
situation: You tell your manager about the results. There is no fuss, and Priya covers for you. Follow-up tests show the nodule is benign and the extra beats are linked to late nights and caffeine. The doctor gives you a plan and stresses sleep. You are relieved, and you also take it as your body's first warning. Back at work, you have to decide how hard to push.

options.text: Reset how you work: fixed hours, with the high-intensity work spread out
Nothing serious showed up, so you fall back into late-night sprints

title: Remote client keeps sending the work back
situation: You wave the chat log to prove you were right. The client is left looking small, and even though they were in the wrong they snap: “This partnership isn’t a courtroom.” Everything after that is spiky. You won the point and lost the relationship.

options.text: Cool things down: move from ‘who was wrong’ to ‘how we get this right’, and propose better sign-off
Insist you did nothing wrong, and wait for them to blink first

title: Pushed on stage at the Christmas party
situation: The Christmas party is in full swing. The host spots you, and your table, colleagues and manager included, starts chanting for you to get up and do something to “get the room going.” You have nothing prepared and this is not your sort of thing, but every eye is on you and someone is already holding out a microphone.

options.text: Take it in good humour: a quick gag or a bit of audience interaction, just enough to lift the room
Smile and say, ‘Thanks, but not tonight’
Shut it down flat with “I’m not doing that”, and let the room go quiet

title: A promotion without a pay rise
situation: You look at it coolly. If the title gives you real experience of leading people or owning a piece of work, and sets up the next pay and promotion conversation, it is worth having. If it is just a vague promise with extra work attached, you should be wary. You take that view into the conversation with your manager.

options.text: Take on the extra responsibility, but press for a clear pay-review date or the resources to match
Take the title and say nothing at all about money

title: Forced ranking: scoring a colleague who is also a friend
situation: Ethan’s bonus is in the normal range. Privately he says he understands. In calibration your manager uses your comments and asks him to write up the incident.

options.text: Help Ethan rework the write-up and keep the friendship
Keep your distance and stay strictly professional

title: Whether to volunteer as lunch-and-learn speaker
situation: The team's lunch-and-learn needs a speaker for the next slot. The topic is callback idempotency, which you have just worked on. Signing up means about 40 minutes of slides, and this week's calendar is already full.

options.text: Volunteer to speak
Suggest that Priya, who knows this area well, gives the talk
Don't sign up. Stay on delivery

title: One umbrella, a downpour, and Jordan at going-home time
situation: The umbrella is small and your shoulders still get wet. On the way Jordan talks about your manager squeezing the timetable lately, and they sound low. At the station they hesitate: “Want to grab a bowl of something hot near mine? On me.” The rain is getting heavier.

options.text: Accept, and listen to how the project is going
Decline and catch the last train home

title: A dependent team is late — do you escalate in the open?
situation: A critical piece of work your project depends on, owned by a sister team, is already two weeks late. Their tech lead says privately they 'need another week' but will not update the official plan. The risk to your project is about to show in an update to senior management. You can keep coordinating quietly, or escalate formally.

options.text: Escalate the risk to senior leadership and ask for a firm delivery commitment
Keep coordinating privately, give them another week's buffer, and prepare a stopgap

title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
situation: After a month of lunching with the team twice a week, your manager stops talking about “mixing in”. Over lunch you learn Warren’s project is being folded into your module, so you have time to prepare.

options.text: Keep to the current pattern
Go to more lunches to stay more visible

title: A dinner that is really a fishing trip for team gossip
situation: Leo is pulled in early and takes it badly. Your manager finds your name in the chat history.

options.text: Apologise and accept the reprimand
Say Sonya tricked it out of you

title: Whether to tell your manager about a health problem
situation: You hide it and push through, and for a while the work gets done. Then, on a critical piece of work, you run out of steam, and people start to speculate.

options.text: Come clean now and adjust the plan
Keep hiding it and gamble that nobody notices

title: A new manager is hired in, and you start again on trust
situation: A clear update and solid delivery make a good first impression, and they start taking your views seriously. Then they ask for something the last manager never would. People mutter in private that it is change for change’s sake.

options.text: Judge the new request on its merits, deliver it well, and add something useful
Join the private muttering that the old way was better

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: You run the rival down in the pitch. One of the panellists turns out to know them, and the room cools: “We asked for your proposal, not a review of someone else’s.” You look small, and it costs you marks.

options.text: Pull it back immediately and return to what your own proposal actually delivers
Keep going on about their past failures

title: A database migration window clashes with peak trading
situation: You are leading the membership database migration from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0, scheduled for Sunday 02:00–06:00. On Friday, product announces that a peak trading period has been brought forward to Monday midnight. Chris, the DBA, says: 'The rollback script is not fully tested. Going ahead is a big risk.'

options.text: Ask to delay the migration and protect peak trading first
Cut testing short and go ahead as planned
Propose dual-write with a two-week canary cutover

title: In-house kernel versus an open-source stack
situation: The platform goes live on the open-source stack on time and the business is pleased. Then a routine security scan flags a problem: this version has an undisclosed candidate CVE, and details are already circulating among a few people internally. If it can be triggered in production, it would hit your core clients. The call is yours.

options.text: Tell security and rush out a fallback from scratch
Sit on the report and bet it will not be triggered soon

title: Caffeine dependence and a broken sleep pattern
situation: You rely more and more on coffee and energy drinks. They get you through the day, then you cannot sleep, and the cycle repeats. Your focus and mood are both getting worse.

options.text: Reset: limit caffeine, keep a regular sleep routine and recover gradually
Keep relying on caffeine and finish what is in front of you first

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You stop the remark without a scene and bring the talk back to the work. The client looks uncomfortable. Chloe is glad someone drew a line. Nobody asks her to repair the relationship. That job belongs to the account lead.

options.text: Leave the client relationship with the account lead, and ask Chloe only what support she wants
Decide you were in the right, and make no effort to repair it

title: The colleague who buys coffee is collecting favours for a lead vote
situation: Harvey brings the team coffees from Pret every day and never takes money. You notice a notebook: “Favours ledger: Chris +2, Ethan +1…” The team is about to pick an acting lead, and Harvey is standing. Today he hands you a larger coffee: “Put in a word for me at the review tonight?”

options.text: Refuse to campaign. In the review, stick to the facts
Agree to talk him up, in return for later support
Warn your manager privately that someone is trading favours for support
Start buying coffees yourself and join the favours game

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: Your manager papers over it, but the client is not satisfied. Your manager asks why you did not explain in the room.

options.text: Reply to the email at once with the facts, and take ownership of the fixes
Excuse it as "not the moment to speak"

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: The hotfix introduces a new conflict. CI goes red.

options.text: Stop the release completely and roll the merge back
Force the hotfix through

title: A restrictive covenant on the way out: take the pay or keep your options
situation: You work through the clauses: scope, payment, and what happens if you breach. You also weigh the risk that your new employer would count as a competitor. Knowing all that, you can negotiate on equal terms: narrow the scope, raise the payment, or simply go somewhere the restriction does not reach.

options.text: Negotiate a narrower scope or a better payment, and sign a version both sides can live with
Choose a direction the restriction does not cover and avoid the dispute altogether

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: Dave was put out by the gentle no that day, but then did the work himself. A week later he hits something that really is beyond him and hesitates to ask you. You hear about it.

options.text: Tell him, 'If you're really stuck, come to me', and help without doing it for him
Keep your distance. You are done being used as spare capacity

title: Pitching against a cheaper rival
situation: You walk through a solid technical design and a cost-of-ownership model that explains the price. The technical panellists nod along. Procurement still stares at the number: “You’re well above the other bid. How do we sell this to our leadership?”

options.text: Offer staged payments plus a measurable ROI model procurement can repeat upstairs
Keep talking technology and dodge the pricing question

title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
situation: Your manager asks you each to write a one-page case for attending, and a director will decide. You both get to work on it. The atmosphere is awkward but still civil.

options.text: Keep the one-pager to business value and what you would bring back, without knocking Jo
Compare the two of you in the one-pager and imply you are the better fit

title: Raising a technical objection on another team's API design
situation: Their owner thanks you for the private heads-up, admits it was an oversight, and is willing to change the design. They add, offhand: "Let's keep this between us — no need to air it in the channel, or it will look as if our review missed it." You need to decide whether to share the finding with the wider teams so others can learn from it.

options.text: Agree the fix in the 1:1, then record the problem and the decision in the design doc
Anonymise it as a "performance review lesson" and share it with both teams

title: Admitting you are not coping, and asking for help
situation: When you come back, colleagues have covered your work and the plan has been moved around your absence. Meanwhile, someone who gritted it out to the end was admitted to hospital with acute anxiety. You can talk about what happened, or keep the details private.

options.text: If you want to, talk about the leave, and suggest the team builds a workload and support check into how it works
Keep it quiet, and prove yourself again through delivery

title: A former colleague asks you for internal company material
situation: A former colleague gets in touch, very friendly, and asks a "small favour": send them some internal material or data. "You've got it to hand. It's not a big deal." The material is company property and covered by confidentiality. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, explain it is confidential company property that can't go outside, and keep things civil
Send the internal material because you feel you can't say no
Send it, plus extra they didn't ask for, to look generous

title: The new manager from outside wants you to inform on the team
situation: The manager hired from outside wants a quick picture of the team and takes you aside: 'You've been here. Tell me how people really are and who has issues. I'll remember you for it.' It could be a chance to be useful. It could also be a trap that makes you the informant.

options.text: Give a fair picture of the team and the work, without informing on anyone or running them down
Embellish complaints about colleagues to please the new manager
Refuse outright and brusquely, even to give a normal briefing

title: A merge conflict wrecks release day
situation: On release day you are merging the release branch. After a long session resolving conflicts, you accidentally pull in untested feature-branch code. CI is green because a flaky test skipped one check.

options.text: Halt the release as soon as you notice and roll the merge back
Carry on with the release and gamble that the code path will not be hit
Quietly hotfix the wrongly merged files out

title: The person next to you wears very strong perfume
situation: Your new neighbour wears very heavy perfume. A morning of it has given you a headache. She clearly loves it, and even asks, "Nice, isn't it?" Saying no might hurt her feelings, but putting up with it is miserable.

options.text: Tell her gently that strong scent gives you headaches, and ask if she could wear less
Praise it insincerely and keep sitting there with a headache
Turn to other colleagues and moan that she "stinks the place out"

title: You notice promotions going to the people who play politics
situation: You have watched this for three years. The fastest riser is Harvey: average technically, but he never misses karaoke, five-a-side or the pub after work. Your technical scores have topped the team for years, yet your promotion still lags. Chris says they also look at “the whole picture”.

options.text: Make more effort socially, without crossing your own lines
Refuse to play along and double down on technical output
Tell Helen, the HR business partner, that the promotion criteria are too vague
Start looking elsewhere and ease off here

title: Your manager asks: individual contributor or management?
situation: You look at yourself honestly. Do you get more from digging into hard technical problems, or from organising people and resources and getting work done through others? Once that is clear, you know which way you lean, and what you would need to build if you took that path. You take the answer back to your manager.

options.text: Choose the path that fits, list the skills you still need, and ask your manager to help you grow into it
See the answer clearly, then dither and refuse to commit

title: Where personal use of work kit stops
situation: The company issues a high-spec workstation and a 4K display. Policy allows 'limited personal use' without saying exactly where the limit is. You have started using the work kit for a personal open-source project that does not compete with the business, and at weekends it soaks up a fair amount of compute. A colleague spots weekend commits from the office IP and jokes, 'So the company is sponsoring your open source now?' You realise it could be misread.

options.text: Stop using work kit for the personal project immediately, and move it onto your own machines
Ask your manager and compliance whether the current use sits inside policy, and get it in writing

title: Named on a department award you did not work on
situation: Your manager is put out: “Fine. Aurora is one name short.” He calls you ungrateful. Aurora goes on to win.

options.text: Put your head down and let next quarter’s delivery speak
Ask HR anonymously whether naming people who did not contribute is allowed

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: Felix pieces the merger together from other sources anyway. Helios goes after your clients with precisely targeted price cuts.

options.text: Tell compliance you may have overstepped the line
Stay silent

title: A leaver asks you to keep work files off the company systems
situation: One evening Felix, who is leaving for a competitor, sends you a link to 8GB of files in cloud storage: “Three years of project scripts and client-contact notes. I wiped the company drive — keep this for me, and don’t upload it here.” Some of the files are scanned client contracts marked Internal. You know his leaver agreement says he must not take business data with him.

options.text: Refuse the files and tell him to use the proper handover
Take the link without opening it, and plan to delete it later
Take it and report it to Information Security

title: Telling the client the project will be late
situation: You were straight with them early. The client is not pleased, but respects that you were professional and took responsibility: 'At least you didn't hide it. I can explain that internally.' Then they push: could you ship a usable core first and the rest next week?

options.text: Check what is feasible, then offer phased delivery: the core first, the rest after
To keep them happy, promise both the core and the full version by the original date

title: Mentoring a graduate who breaks things
situation: You took responsibility in public and Sam is hugely grateful. That afternoon your manager pulls you into a meeting room: 'We're already over our incident quota. Group wants a named person on the accountability report. If you keep this on yourself, the team can't carry it. I suggest you sign the draft that puts the main fault on Sam. I'll try to sort Sam's conversion to permanent another way.' They slide a mostly written template across. Asking for a name to fill a quota is poor management. A fair account of an incident sets out what happened and who did what.

options.text: Sign the draft and put the main fault on Sam
Rewrite it to match what happened: who skipped review, and which check in the process failed

title: A metrics problem, ten minutes before the briefing
situation: Your manager’s face tightens. They drop the slide and go with +12%. The VP asks why it is lower than the figure in last week’s comms. Afterwards your manager says: “Check this a day ahead next time.”

options.text: Offer to follow up with the VP on how the metric is defined
Leave it there so your manager is not made to look small

title: Do you say the code was AI-generated?
situation: Later the team finds bugs nobody had spotted in AI-generated code elsewhere, and starts checking which changes were labelled. Your pull request is dug out of the history.

options.text: Go to your manager, admit you did not label it, and say you should have thought it through
Wait to be asked, then stress that there was no clear rule at the time

title: A collaborator shifts the blame in a meeting
situation: You and Chloe share delivery on a client project. In the weekly meeting the client complains about repeated API changes and thin test coverage. Chloe speaks first: “The API design was mainly theirs. I worked to the version they gave me. Testing was held up on their team too.” In fact the changes came from the client changing their mind three times, and you emailed several times for a test environment without getting one. Your manager and the client both look at you. You need to respond in the room.

options.text: Walk through the timeline and the email trail, and set out who owned what
Take some of the blame for now to steady the client, and leave Chloe for later
Hit back in the room: Chloe did not provide the integration environment on time
Stay silent and ask your manager to unpick it

title: Asking for remote work or a steadier role for family reasons
situation: Your family needs more of you. You are thinking of asking to work remotely or to move to a steadier, less intense role, but you worry it will look like a lack of ambition and hurt your promotion chances.

options.text: Be clear about the trade-off: make a formal request and commit to keeping your work up to standard
Make a vague request, because you want the easier setup but fear looking unambitious
Say nothing and keep grinding as you are

title: A leaver asks you to keep work files off the company systems
situation: Three months later competitor Halcyon Tech quotes your clients with unusual precision. InfoSec is checking access logs. Felix once logged into a drive you hold.

options.text: Come forward and say you received a link you had not yet deleted
Deny knowing anything

title: An undeclared relationship that looks like a conflict of interest
situation: Three months later that report is promoted. Other candidates feel the process was unfair and cannot say so. In an exit interview, one of them mentions 'an undeclared conflict in the promotion review'. HR traces it back and asks whether you knew.

options.text: Admit what you saw, and explain you were not sure at the time whether you should report it
Deny knowing anything. Insist you never saw anything unusual

title: A manager-free channel shares a screenshot of your boss
situation: In the Lynx late-night Slack channel, where no managers are allowed, someone posts a screenshot of Chris tearing into people: "If you can't even do this, what bonus do you think you deserve?" The next message: "Thoughts? Should we reply as a group?" You're in the channel. Passing a copy to HR, a staff representative, a union or a solicitor so they can deal with the complaint is not itself a disciplinary matter. Spreading it to people who have nothing to do with the complaint is another matter.

options.text: Ask them to stop spreading it, keep the evidence the target needs, and raise it through a grievance or staff rep
Join in and have a moan
Leave the channel and stay out of it
Message Chris privately about team morale, without saying how you know

title: A former colleague at a competitor fishes for intel
situation: Former colleague Felix has moved to Helios. He once referred you into this job. Over dinner he asks, "Has Lynx locked the team merger yet? What's the Polaris budget?" His contract forbids him from fishing for commercial information from people who still work here.

options.text: Refuse, and keep the chat to personal matters
Share non-confidential industry gossip
Tell him about the draft merger plan, as a way of repaying the favour

title: Anonymous feedback — do you own up?
situation: Your manager appears to accept the denial, but their expression says otherwise. Later, chances that would have been yours go to other people. The explanation is that 'others need more stretch'.

options.text: Find a better moment and admit you denied it to protect how anonymous feedback is meant to work
Live with it, let the work speak, and trust time to clear the misunderstanding

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: The temperature in your corner of the open-plan office is a running sore. Hugh always feels hot and throws the windows open as soon as he arrives. Maya always feels cold, so she shuts them and turns the radiator up. It can go back and forth several times a day. Today they snap at each other in front of everyone. Nobody else wants to step in, and everyone looks at you: you are fairly neutral, and people listen to you.

options.text: Propose a middle temperature, plus a small extra for each: a desk fan, a draught screen
Make the call: set the temperature most people like, and tell them both to stop
Keep your head down and work. It's not your problem

title: Whether to join a cross-team architecture review — and how hard to push
situation: You go in deep and raise a core objection to one design: they plan to introduce a framework that has not been used at scale inside the company, which carries a maintenance risk. Their owner disagrees in the meeting, fairly bluntly. The chair suggests you carry on the discussion afterwards. You need to decide what to do next.

options.text: Write a full risk assessment and submit it formally to the tech committee
Defer to their judgement and file your comments as an appendix

title: Choosing a path for a legacy service hitting its limits
situation: A core order service you own has been live for three years and is reaching its performance limit. Monitoring shows QPS already at 80% of the original design limit, and in another quarter or two normal growth will probably overwhelm it. Your manager has given you three months to propose a path, without saying which one. You could rewrite it on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation, refactor it in stages on the current architecture, or ship the smallest performance patches that will carry you through this cycle.

options.text: Rewrite on a modern framework as a three-to-five-year foundation
Refactor in stages on the current architecture
Ship the smallest performance patches and ride out this cycle

title: Client makes an inappropriate joke at dinner
situation: You laugh along to keep the client sweet. To everyone watching, that is taking part. Chloe is finished with you and will not work with you if she can help it. It gets round the team that you have no line when a deal is on the table. Your manager hears, and starts to doubt your judgement. Whatever goodwill you gained with the client, you have lost as much inside the company.

options.text: Own it: apologise properly to Chloe and admit you were out of order
Brush it off as ‘just dinner banter’ and insist you did nothing wrong

title: A drunk colleague at the Christmas party
situation: You stay for the show. Will fully unravels in front of your manager, becomes office comedy the next day, and gets a formal conversation about it. He later finds out you were right there watching and did not pull him back, and he is gutted. You have lost someone who could have become a friend.

options.text: Apologise to Will, and put in a fair word for him with your manager
Shrug it off — you didn’t pour the drinks

title: The office war over windows and heating
situation: You kept your head down. The two of them dug in further and ended up asking your manager to referee. Your manager frowns: 'You can't sort out something this small?' Everyone who could have stepped in and didn't, you included, now looks as if it is nothing to do with them. The atmosphere is awkward for days.

options.text: Step in late with a middle option so both of them have a way out
Stay out of it. It's still not your problem

title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
situation: Sienna does not buy. She tells her husband, who “anonymously” discusses it in an industry group chat. The story reaches HR.

options.text: Tell HR the truth about how the leak spread
Deny it was you

title: Thanking a colleague from the next team who went out of their way
situation: Last week a nasty bug in a barely maintained legacy submodule had you stuck for two days. Chris, a senior engineer on the next team, sat at your desk for a whole afternoon and helped you find and fix it. Nobody required them to spend that long. It is Friday, and you want to say thank you. You could take them out for a good lunch on you, around £30–40. You could write a formal recognition note on the intranet, copied to Chris and their manager, recording their high-quality cross-team help. Or you could do nothing special now and make a point of helping them next time they need it.

options.text: Take them out for lunch privately, straight away
Write a formal recognition note and copy their manager
Do nothing special for now and help them next time they need it

title: Whether to share the method you have kept to yourself
situation: The post takes off. Lauren uses the write-up to improve the system, and your manager asks you to standardise it across the team.

options.text: Lead training for the whole group and step up as the technical expert
Worry about being replaced and start holding things back again

title: A security hole that would be expensive to fix
situation: The release slips two weeks. Sales complain about lost deals. At the exec meeting the CEO asks whether a medium-severity issue is worth several million pounds of revenue. The CISO backs you in the meeting, then tells you privately that they held the line this time but want a more balanced answer from you next time.

options.text: Start a shift-left process, so similar issues are found much earlier
Soften your stance, and promise to be more 'pragmatic' in balancing security against the business

title: Health check returning the wrong status
situation: Your load-balancer health-check endpoint returns 200, but the body says status is degraded, so traffic still hits unhealthy instances.

options.text: Fix the endpoint now and check the other services
Fix this service only
Leave it for on-call

title: You overhear a redundancy list that includes a friend
situation: From a toilet cubicle you hear a VP and the HR director discussing the Q2 redundancy list: “…Ethan is in the consultation pool after the Lynx Wallet incident, package would be a standard redundancy…” Ethan is your tennis partner and helped you move last week. They wash their hands and leave, unaware you were there. The list has not been announced.

options.text: Tell no one and act as if you never heard it
Hint that Ethan should keep his head down and not resign in a hurry
Tell him he is on the list and what the package looks like
Tell Ethan only about the published redundancy process and support channels, and nothing you overheard

title: Emergency hotfix — do you skip the process?
situation: The full process takes three hours. The client's live event is badly hit. The sales VP asks openly whether engineering's response time matches what the business needs. The wash-up shows the degraded mode did not fully cover the missing function.

options.text: In the wash-up, admit the process was too rigid, and propose a graded response for future emergencies
Stress quality first, and point out that a hotfix introducing a new fault would have cost more

title: Your idea is pitched first by someone else
situation: In a team brainstorm you suggest a design, but it gets little attention. Two weeks later a colleague pitches almost the same idea in a wider meeting, with some of the same wording. A VP likes it and asks them to lead it. You cannot tell whether they got there independently or borrowed yours. Either way, they are now seen as the person who proposed it and will take most of the credit.

options.text: Speak to them privately afterwards, mention the discussion two weeks ago, and check where the idea came from
Share your earlier thinking with the team, without directly challenging their claim to the idea

title: A newly hired VP talks to you alone for ten minutes on day one
situation: Two weeks later Hale does not follow up one-to-one. The gossip cools. Chris is back to normal.

options.text: Let your project results strengthen your position
Moan that it was a nine-day wonder

title: A colleague who keeps handing you his work
situation: You took the lot again. At the month-end review your own work is unfinished and your manager pulls you up on it, while Dave is praised for 'on-time delivery' of work you produced. The unfairness and the performance pressure hit you at the same time.

options.text: Give your manager the facts on how the work was really split, and redraw the line
Swallow it. A falling-out is not worth it

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: At the company's quarterly leadership review, you have to report on a milestone for a project you own. The execs are short of time and only want conclusions and risks. They have no interest in process. There is still an unresolved risk on the project, and progress is only 'broadly on track'. You have ten minutes.

options.text: Lead with the conclusion: key results first, then the risk and the plan to deal with it
Give only the good news: hide the risk and stick to highlights throughout
Walk through the process in detail, still not reaching the point ten minutes in

title: A milestone briefing for the execs
situation: You only talked about highlights, and the execs came away impressed on the day. Two months later the risk materialises, the damage spreads, and leadership digs out the briefing notes: 'Why was there not a word about risk?' You are on the back foot.

options.text: Run a review, own the bad call, and show the fix already in place
Argue that 'nobody could have seen this then'

title: Dismissed in a team meeting as "just engineering work"
situation: You do not push back in the meeting. Afterwards you take a few colleagues for coffee and spell out the project's value and their part in it, and morale lifts. Your manager does not raise it again, and does not correct the remark in public either. You need to decide whether to take the point further.

options.text: Use the next meeting's pre-read to put business value in a summary your manager will see
Keep encouraging colleagues privately and do not raise it with your manager again

title: The client adds three things 'while we're here'
situation: You agreed to all of it. The client is pleased for now, the plan is wrecked, and quality on the original features is starting to slip. Encouraged, the client keeps 'mentioning in passing' more work, and the scope creep has no end in sight.

options.text: Stop it now: tell the client and your manager where things stand, and reset scope and change control
Keep taking whatever comes, and have the team work late to carry it

title: A new colleague with no sense of privacy
situation: One sentence stops Lou in her tracks. She goes red, barely speaks to you for days, and tells other people you are 'quite fierce'. You held the line, but a new colleague was rattled and her settling in took a knock.

options.text: Find a moment to soften it: you just don't discuss your private life, and it wasn't personal
Don't soften it. The boundary matters more than her feelings

title: Vaping at the neighbouring desk
situation: After lunch, Robin at the next desk is vaping again. The cloud hangs over the open plan. The office rule is no vaping inside. You were hoping to concentrate this afternoon.

options.text: Smile and quietly remind him vaping inside isn't allowed and the shelter is downstairs
Frown and put up with it without saying anything
Post a snide note in the channel: "some people might show a bit of consideration"

title: You overhear an unpublished project naming you
situation: You hear budget and competitor detail. Miles turns: “Who’s there?”

options.text: Step out and say you were just passing, without admitting you listened
Step out, say you heard your name, and ask whether this is a normal process
